title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction.
We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone.
We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at this https URL.

report.summary: MCPHallu benchmarks 14 frontier agents on 36 live MCP servers and finds persistent reasoning, execution and memory hallucinations — with recognizing infeasible goals the weakest spot.
report.background: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become the de facto plumbing for connecting LLM agents to external tools, letting a single agent discover and call functions across many servers at runtime. But as MCP deployments spread, evaluation has lagged: most benchmarks score only whether a task was completed, and when they do diagnose failures, they do so after the run rather than deliberately engineering the situations that provoke hallucination. That leaves teams unable to tell whether a weak score reflects a bad model, a bad tool description, or a bad environment. MCPHallu, from a research team publishing on arXiv, attacks this by treating hallucination as a structural property of task design. It builds tasks with deliberate traps along three axes — reasoning, execution and memory — so that a specific failure mode becomes the dominant risk, and it runs them against production MCP servers rather than mocks. The result is the first subtype-level diagnostic picture of how frontier agents misbehave when tools get adversarial.
key_points: Three-axis diagnostic design: MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains, each with a structural trigger that makes one of four failure subtypes dominant — Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse or Context Forgetting — so results can be analyzed per failure mode instead of as one aggregate success rate.

Unreachable Goal is the glaring weakness: average score there drops to 0.458 and only 23.2% of runs pass. Rather than reporting that a goal cannot be achieved, agents keep firing off tool calls or simply claim they finished the job — a dangerous failure in real deployments.

Model rankings are unstable across failure types: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average depending on subtype, and Branch Collapse performance is essentially uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal performance (r = -0.12). There is no single 'hallucination score'.

Overall performance is mediocre at scale: across 5,012 trajectories from 14 frontier agents from 8 vendors, running on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers, the mean score is 0.642 on a 0-1 scale — meaning roughly a third of behaviour still goes wrong under trap conditions.
report.impact: For the AI industry, MCPHallu shifts agent evaluation from 'did it finish?' to 'how does it fail?' — a framing that matters as enterprises start buying agents on benchmark claims. Vendors can no longer hide behind a single success number, since a model that tops one subtype may rank near the bottom on another. For developers, the four subtypes map directly onto engineering work: explicit feasibility checks before tool loops, state tracking to prevent context forgetting, per-tool validation to avoid misuse, and search strategies that do not collapse down one branch. The Unreachable Goal result is the most actionable warning — agents that falsely report success are worse than agents that fail loudly. For regular users, it means agent demos will keep overstating reliability until these guardrails become standard.
report.tools: Start with the MCPHallu benchmark itself (arXiv 2611.07689, released with code and data) to reproduce or extend the subtypes. For hands-on MCP debugging, use MCP Inspector and the official MCP SDKs (TypeScript/Python). Pair them with general agent-evaluation harnesses such as Inspect AI or Promptfoo to build your own trap tasks, and add runtime guardrails (LangGraph interrupts, schema validation, explicit 'goal infeasible' exit paths) to catch the Unreachable Goal and Tool Misuse failures the paper highlights.
